title: Properties Graph
statement:
`properties` is an `n x m` grid of integers (every row has length `m`), and `k` is an integer. Picture an undirected graph with one node for each row index `0, 1, ..., n - 1`. Two different nodes `i` and `j` are joined by an edge exactly when the rows `properties[i]` and `properties[j]` have at least `k` **distinct** values in common; a value that appears several times in a row still counts once.

Return how many connected components this graph has.
notes:
## Intuition

The work splits in two: decide which pairs of rows are joined, then count the pieces the graph falls into. Turning each row into a `Set` of its values removes repeats, so the number of shared values is just the members of one set that the other set `has`. Instead of storing the graph and searching it, union-find merges rows as soon as an edge is found: start with `n` separate components, and every merge of two different components removes one. Storing the whole adjacency matrix and running a depth-first search also works; union-find needs no stored edges and can skip pairs that are already connected.

## Approach

1. Build `distinct[i]`, the set of values in row `i`.
2. Give each row its own tree (`parent[i] = i`) and start `components` at `n`.
3. `find(node)` walks up to the root of `node`'s tree, pointing nodes at their grandparents on the way to keep trees shallow.
4. For every pair `i < j`, look up `rootI` and `rootJ`. If they are equal the rows are already connected, so skip the pair.
5. Otherwise count `shared`, the values of `distinct[i]` that `distinct[j]` also has. If `shared >= k`, hang `rootI` under `rootJ` and decrease `components`.
6. Return `components`.

## Example 1, step by step

With `k = 1` the sets are `{1, 2}`, `{1}`, `{3, 4}`, `{4, 5}`, `{5, 6}`, `{7}`, and `components` starts at 6. Pair (0, 1) shares the value 1, so the rows merge: 5. Pair (2, 3) shares 4: 4. Pair (2, 4) shares nothing, but pair (3, 4) shares 5, which joins row 4 to rows 2 and 3: 3. No other pair shares a value, so the answer is `3`: rows {0, 1}, {2, 3, 4} and {5}.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n² · m): each of the n(n - 1)/2 pairs scans at most m distinct values, and `find` is nearly constant with path halving.
- Space: O(n · m) for the sets and O(n) for `parent`.

## Pitfalls

- Count distinct values: `[1, 1]` and `[1, 1]` share one value, not two (Example 3).
- Components follow chains of edges: rows 2 and 4 of Example 1 share nothing yet end up together through row 3.
- Decrease `components` only when two different roots merge; counting every qualifying pair would subtract too much.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `distinct` | `distinct[i]` is the set of values in row `i` |
| `parent` | union-find parent of each row; a root is its own parent |
| `node` | the row `find` is walking up from |
| `components` | number of separate trees so far |
| `i`, `j` | the pair of rows being compared |
| `rootI`, `rootJ` | the roots of rows `i` and `j` |
| `shared` | how many distinct values the two rows have in common |
